title: Individual Discovery

skills.blurb: Choose an ordered work item, then work through its questions and artifact with your agent.
Review the capture disclosure, then check identity, push access, hook wiring, and capture.
Check every work item, then choose an unfinished one by number, ID, or title to continue.
Commit and push what you have, record the session's decisions, and confirm it is safe to close.
Check every work item, push the commit and submission tag, then confirm the receipt in OTUS.

components.label: Problem Finding & Vetting
components.notes: One markdown file with TWO sub-sections: (1) Problem finding — a list of 20+ problem areas, each naming a customer and their needs/pain points, no solutions; (2) Problem vetting — a structured framework applied to that list, producing one top problem. Restored 2026-08-26 (cs50g07b) from the 2025F deliverable doc, where it was D1a PROBLEM FINDING; it had been stripped out of the 2026F rebuild. Its output is a SOFT prerequisite for D1b and D1c: the coaching orders it first and every downstream item's questions confirm the chosen problem, but nothing blocks a student who works ahead. Detection stays file-level; quality of the framework is the instructor's call at grading.

components.label: Opportunity Recognition
components.notes: One markdown narrative with THREE sub-sections: (1) JTBD analysis, (2) Customer insights (starts with a real interview; synthesis from the transcript, with quotes), (3) Market sizing (light TAM/SAM). Was D1a until 2026-08-26, when Problem Finding & Vetting was restored ahead of it and took the D1a slot (cs50g07b). Renamed from 'Opportunity Brief' and reduced from four sections on 2026-08-13 (cn80tkzn): the former section (1) 'Problem Statement & Opportunity' moved to the pitch, because problem/whom/why is what a pitch is made of. D1b is the ANALYSIS; D1c is the ARGUMENT. The sub-sections are headings within this one file (format truth), so detection stays file-level.

components.label: Pitch — the case + content draft
components.notes: The in-repo content draft of the pitch (render-agnostic). Required regardless of how the final deck is rendered - keeps the substance observed (handoff 4.3 guardrail). As of 2026-08-13 this ALSO carries the case itself - problem, whom, why now, received from the analysis - stated as components rather than a formal 'problem statement', with no solution named. This is where `opportunity_recommendation_structure` is primarily assessed. Deliberately NO slide-by-slide guidance: a prescribed order produces identical decks and a boring presentation day; choosing what to lead with (quantitative backing for an intuitive problem, storytelling for a niche one) is part of the assessed judgment. Was D1b until the 2026-08-26 renumber.

components.label: Pitch deck / presentation link
components.notes: <=6 slides AND <=2 min total incl. mixed media - both hard caps, with NO prescribed slide order (2026-08-13); student choice on media mix (Google Slides, deployed reveal.js/Marp, or a recording). The link is pasted in submission.md. link_kind:presentation = any hosted presentation link — ratified 2026-06-24 as an addition to the link_kind vocabulary (contract §3.2).

questions: What problem areas have you noticed in your own everyday life, or in products you would like to correct or disrupt?
What have friends, family or former colleagues complained about recently?
Which broad shifts — technological, economic, sociocultural, sociopolitical — are opening gaps nobody has filled yet?
For each line: who is the prospective customer, and what is their need or pain point? A problem area with no customer named is not yet on the list.
Have you got to twenty? If the list is stalling, switch approach — bottoms-up (your own pain points) and top-down (broad shifts) surface different problems.

work_items.title: Problem Finding
complete_when: At least 20 problem areas are listed.
Each line names a prospective customer along with their needs and/or pain points.
No solution is named or hinted at anywhere in the list.
The list is the student's own work rather than the shipped prompt.

questions: What criteria are you assessing these problems against, and why those?
What scale are you using — high/medium/low, 1-5, something else?
For viability, what is your intended customer's willingness to pay to have the problem solved? Assess the problem, not an assumed solution.
For feasibility, what is the nature of the problem? Problems that are societal, systemic, or physically hard are inherently low-feasibility, and that is worth saying.
Which problem came out on top, and if there was a tie, how did you break it?

work_items.title: Problem Vetting
complete_when: A structured framework is applied to the list, with the criteria and scale stated.
One top problem is named as the one being carried forward.
The rationale for that choice is visible, including how any tie was broken.
The section is the student's own work rather than the shipped prompt.

questions: Which problem did you pick in D1a-2? This analysis runs on that problem — confirm it before you start.
Who is the customer you have in mind, specifically enough that you could name someone who fits?
What outcome are they trying to reach — stated as a job they want done, not a feature they would use?
What do they do about it today, and where does that break down?
Which of the functional, emotional, or social dimensions materially change the picture here, and how? Skip any that do not earn their place.

work_items.title: JTBD Analysis
complete_when: The analysis is explicitly about the problem selected in D1a-2.
The primary job is stated as an outcome the customer wants rather than a solution or feature.
The dimensions that materially matter (functional, emotional, or social) are covered, with no requirement to run through all three.
The section is the student's own prose rather than the shipped prompt.

questions: Have you run the interview yet? This section starts with a real conversation — there is nothing to synthesize before that.
Who did you talk to, and what is their relationship to the problem you selected in D1a-2?
Where are your notes or transcript? The synthesis is done from the real record of the conversation, not from memory.
What did you actually hear that you did not expect going in?
Which quote carries the most weight, and who said it — their words, not a paraphrase?

work_items.title: Customer Insights
complete_when: A real interview has been conducted, and the notes or transcript are kept in the repo as supporting material.
The synthesis is drawn from that transcript rather than from recollection.
At least one direct quote is included and attributed.
The section is the student's own prose rather than the shipped prompt.

questions: How many potential customers are there, and how did you arrive at that count?
What would they plausibly pay, and on what basis?
Is this an established market or an emergent one? For an established market you can anchor to current revenue; for an emergent one you are projecting, and the assumptions carry the weight.
Which segment of that total could realistically be served — the SAM — and why that boundary?
Where did each figure come from? Name the source, or say it is a first-principles estimate.

work_items.title: Market Sizing
complete_when: A light TAM and SAM estimate are both present.
The reasoning behind the numbers is visible, not just the final figures.
Sources or first-principles assumptions are named for the figures used.

questions: Stated as your customer's problem rather than the absence of a product, what is broken?
Whom is it for — a specific segment, not 'everyone who...'?
Why now: what has actually changed in technology, cost, regulation, or behaviour?
Which parts of this are carried over from your D1b analysis, and which are new claims?

work_items.title: The Case
complete_when: The problem is stated as the customer's problem.
A specific segment is named for whom it is.
A why-now claim naming what changed is present.
No solution or feature list is named.

questions: Is your problem closer to intuitive (the room recognises it instantly) or niche (nobody has met it)? Where between the two does yours sit?
Given that, does your pitch lead with quantitative backing or with a story — and why that choice for this problem?
CONCISE: two minutes is not a lot of time. Of everything you compiled across D1a and D1b, what earns a place on a slide, and what gets cut?
COMPELLING: what is the one or two things you want your classmates to take away? Where is the a-ha moment in your two minutes?
CONVINCING: which qualitative or quantitative evidence best makes your case, and what would a sceptic in the room push back on?
What goes on each slide, up to six? Sketch them in order.
What medium are you building in (Google Slides, a deployed reveal.js or Marp deck, or a recording), and what is the link once it exists?

work_items.title: Your Slides
complete_when: A slide sketch of no more than six slides is present in pitch/outline.md.
The plan is shaped for this problem rather than a generic template.
A real presentation link is pasted into the Presentation line of submission.md.

_completion_model_note: Two completion vocabularies coexist here on purpose, with different consumers. components[].detect is machine-checkable PRESENCE (file_nonempty, glob_nonempty, tag_exists, link_in_file), evaluated server-side by OTUS's completeness check — it answers 'does the artifact exist'. work_items[].complete_when is prose EVIDENCE read in-repo by /otus-status and /otus-instructions, per work item — it answers 'is this particular piece of thinking actually done'. They sit at different granularity (one file can carry several work items) and neither can replace the other: a detector cannot tell a filled-in section from the shipped prompt, and prose criteria are not evaluable outside an agent. Neither is a quality rubric; quality is the instructor's call at grading.
